title: Australia imported 102 toads in 1935; now there are over 200 million
body: In June 1935, 102 cane toads were shipped from Hawaii to Gordonvale to eat beetles that were damaging sugar cane; by March 1937 some 62,000 captive-bred toadlets had been released. There is **no evidence they ever dented the beetle numbers**, but the toads thrived: by 2011 they were estimated at over 200 million. Their skin toxin kills native predators that try to eat them, from northern quolls to goannas and snakes, and the front is speeding up, from about 40 km a year in 1994 to about 60 by 2014, helped by toads at the front evolving longer legs.

left.label: The plan
left.text: The toads would eat the grey-backed cane beetle and French’s beetle, pests of sugar cane.

right.label: What happened
right.text: No evidence they affected beetle numbers. Native predators that bite the toxic toads, such as northern quolls, die.

slides.question: How many captive-bred toadlets had been released by March 1937?
slides.explanation: Some 62,000 toadlets were bred in captivity and released within two years of the first 102 arriving.

slides.heading: From 102 toads to 200 million
slides.note: The 2011 figure is an estimate; the first 102 were shipped from Hawaii in June 1935

events.text: 102 toads arrive from Hawaii; released around Cairns, Gordonvale and Innisfail
Front advancing about 40 km a year
About 60 km a year, with longer-legged toads leading

slides.heading: Which one isn’t a victim of the toad’s toxin?
slides.explanation: Quolls, goannas and snakes die when they bite a cane toad. The cane beetle was the pest the toads were imported to eat, and there is no evidence they dented its numbers.
